# Linear Algebra Fundamentals

**The central question:** How can we understand a transformation of many numbers by studying only a few basic directions?

This is a new second-level category under **Mathematics**, based on your uploaded *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, **second edition**, by **Ivan Savov**.

::: {.callout-note}
## Source boundary

Your PDF is the **152-page extended book preview**, not the complete 596-page book. I used its introduction, published table of contents and available excerpts to preserve the nine-chapter sequence. These 24 lessons are **original explanations** and independent miniature examples; chapters not fully present in the preview are treated as syllabus-guided expansion, not claims about unseen full-book pages.
:::

## The recurring two-direction example

A tablet projects an arrow onto a wall. You discover that a horizontal unit arrow becomes (2,1), and a vertical unit arrow becomes (1,−1). If the mapping is linear, what happens to arrow (3,2)?

$$
T(3,2)=3T(1,0)+2T(0,1)=3(2,1)+2(1,-1)=(8,1)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** T is the tablet-to-wall transformation; (3,2) is the input arrow; (1,0) and (0,1) are the two standard basis arrows; the coefficients 3 and 2 say how much of each direction to combine.

**Substitute numbers:** Horizontal contribution 3×(2,1)=(6,3). Vertical contribution 2×(1,−1)=(2,−2). Adding gives (8,1). These are exactly the coordinates we would obtain by matrix multiplication.

**Why?** Any two-dimensional arrow is a combination of the two basis directions. Linearity says the transformation preserves these combinations. This one idea connects **vectors, matrices, linear transformations, basis, rank and eigenvectors**.

## The nine learning stages

1. [**Math Fundamentals — Before Vectors**](01-math-foundations/index.qmd) — 2 worked lessons. Book Chapter 1 revisits equations, numbers, functions, geometry, vectors and complex numbers. Our two worked chapters isolate the prerequisites used throughout this path.
2. [**Introduction to Linear Algebra — Vectors and Matrices**](02-intro-linear-algebra/index.qmd) — 3 worked lessons. Book Chapter 2 introduces definitions, vector operations, matrix operations and linearity. Think of vectors as arrows and matrices as rules for moving arrows.
3. [**Computational Linear Algebra — Calculate With Matrices**](03-computational-linear-algebra/index.qmd) — 3 worked lessons. Book Chapter 3 covers row reduction, matrix equations, multiplication, determinants and inverses. Each operation answers a precise question.
4. [**Geometric Linear Algebra — Spaces and Projections**](04-geometric-linear-algebra/index.qmd) — 3 worked lessons. Book Chapter 4 relates points, lines, planes, projections, vector spaces and bases. Geometry turns symbols into directions you can imagine.
5. [**Linear Transformations — How Rules Change Vectors**](05-linear-transformations/index.qmd) — 3 worked lessons. Book Chapter 5 develops linear maps, their matrix representations, basis changes and the invertible matrix theorem. A map is defined by what it does to a basis.
6. [**Theoretical Linear Algebra — Eigenvectors and Structure**](06-theoretical-linear-algebra/index.qmd) — 3 worked lessons. Book Chapter 6 moves into eigenvectors, special matrices, abstract spaces, Gram–Schmidt and decompositions. The abstract ideas grow from ordinary arrows.
7. [**Applications — Use the Mathematics**](07-applications/index.qmd) — 3 worked lessons. Book Chapter 7 applies linear algebra to chemistry, economics, circuits, graphs, optimisation, least squares, graphics, codes and Fourier analysis. Our first examples use fitting, rotation and graph walks.
8. [**Probability Theory — Probability as a Vector**](08-probability/index.qmd) — 2 worked lessons. Book Chapter 8 links probability distributions, Markov chains and PageRank with vectors and stochastic matrices.
9. [**Quantum Mechanics — Complex Vectors and Measurements**](09-quantum-mechanics/index.qmd) — 2 worked lessons. Book Chapter 9 uses Dirac notation and quantum mechanics to apply inner products and linear transformations in a complex vector space.

## The learning rule

Every lesson follows **one question → intuition → an exact formula → immediate symbol definitions → actual numerical substitution → explanation → limitation → a short exercise**. You should be able to reproduce the calculation with a pencil.

The mathematics is the primary lesson; programming is only a verification aid. Try the [one-file Python calculations](examples/index.qmd) after you understand the worked mathematics.
